entities.name: Fundamento de Esperanto
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The "Fundamento de Esperanto," published in 1905 by L. L. Zamenhof, serves as the foundational text for the constructed international language Esperanto, emerging from the linguistic aspirations of its creator to foster global communication and understanding. This text was significant not only for its innovative approach to language but also for its timely emergence amidst the rising tides of nationalism in Europe, which sought to bridge cultural divides across diverse populations. Zamenhof, a Polish-Jewish physician, envisioned Esperanto as a means to transcend ethnic tensions and promote peace, thus marking it as a transformative movement in linguistic history.

The book meticulously outlines the grammar and vocabulary of Esperanto, providing a comprehensive framework that was intended to be simple yet expressive. It was drafted during the first Universal Esperanto Congress held in Boulogne-sur-Mer, France, where Zamenhof's vision gained traction among early adopters and linguists. The text's declaration in Boulogne emphasized that the "Fundamento" would be the only obligatory authority over the language, establishing Zamenhof as a central figure in its development. This formalization allowed Esperanto to flourish, with translations of literary works and the establishment of an international community dedicated to its usage.

The legacy of the "Fundamento de Esperanto" extends far beyond its initial publication, influencing language movements and intercultural dialogue throughout the 20th century. Its impact can be seen in the establishment of Esperanto as a living language, with an estimated 2 million speakers worldwide today, as well as in the formation of numerous organizations that advocate for its use. The notion of a universal language continues to resonate, as it challenges language barriers and fosters a sense of global citizenship, reflecting Zamenhof's enduring vision for peace and understanding among peoples.
